clue.text: Broken toe? A Band-Aid? It could work!

indicators.note: something broken is smashed out of its shape, so the letters that follow are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these words, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: Someone with an injured toe wonders hopefully whether a sticking plaster will do the trick.
explanation.walkthrough: A Band-Aid is a sticking plaster. The question marks are surface dressing and play no part in the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a plan is worth trying amounts to calling it promising, the reaction 'it could work' expresses exactly that.

clue.text: Informant poking dubious charity

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing a charity rather than a noun

indicators.note: a dubious arrangement is a doubtful, unreliable one, telling us the preceding letters are not in their true order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A police informer is sniffing around a shady charitable organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Charities are organisations that are not run to generate profits for owners, so the adjective describes their legal status.

clue.text: Rubbish learner abandoned three times

indicators.note: whatever is abandoned is left behind, so the learner's letter is dropped from the word for the multiple

blocks.note: L is the learner plate on a car
threefold

explanation.surface: A learner driver gives up after failing a test three times, calling the whole thing rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Take L out of TRIPLE to leave TRIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe, literally a cow's stomach lining, is an informal word for nonsense or worthless talk.

clue.text: Disney's classic tear-jerker switched on for little one

indicators.note: switching the two letters of the short word swaps their positions, so it is read the other way round

blocks.note: the Disney film famous for the death of the young deer's mother
taken as written

explanation.surface: A parent puts on a weepy old Disney film for a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switched on' reads like turning on the television, but only the little word 'on' gets switched round.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambino is Italian for a baby or small child, used in English for a little one.

clue.text: Experimented, got bad back and haemorrhaged!

indicators.note: going back means reading the preceding word from its end to its start

blocks.note: taken as written
lost blood heavily

explanation.surface: A reckless scientist's experiment went wrong: a bad back and a bleed.
explanation.walkthrough: BAD reversed is DAB; add BLED for DABBLED.
explanation.definitionFit: To dabble is to try something casually and superficially, much like experimenting without commitment.

clue.text: Mind your head in 12?

definitions.note: a description of what the answer is found in, the filling of a 12-across

blocks.note: first meaning: a warning to crouch low under a beam
second meaning: the soft feathers used to fill bedding, here the quilt at 12-across

explanation.surface: A warning sign at a low doorway, apparently placed inside a bedroom item.
explanation.walkthrough: 12-across is DUVET; DUCK DOWN is both the order to stoop and the soft feather filling of a quilt.
explanation.definitionFit: Stooping to avoid a low beam is what 'mind your head' urges, and quilts are traditionally stuffed with waterfowl feathers.

clue.text: Everywhere is very disorganised

blocks.note: first meaning: in every location
second meaning: in a complete muddle

explanation.surface: Clutter is everywhere: the place is a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means scattered in every location and also, figuratively, chaotic and confused.

clue.text: Working class pocketing drug balances

indicators.note: working here means being reshaped or processed, so the letters of the next word are rearranged
to pocket something is to put it inside, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: taken as written
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: Members of the working class are caught carrying drugs, with scales to weigh them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working class' looks like a single phrase, but 'Working' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Scales and balances are both instruments used for weighing things, the old two-pan type especially.

clue.text: Put an end to hard liquor

blocks.note: first meaning: to stamp out a rumour or plan
second meaning: whisky distilled in Scotland

explanation.surface: A call to stop drinking spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour is to quash it decisively, and the same word names the whisky made north of the border.

clue.text: Administer religious rite to defraud business

blocks.note: to swindle
a company

explanation.surface: A priest's ritual is being used to cheat a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Confirmation is a church sacrament, and a bishop who confirms someone performs that ceremony on them.

clue.text: Rural gripe after bureau cleared out

indicators.note: clearing out a cupboard empties its contents, leaving only the outside shell of the word
after places the word for gripe behind the other piece in the answer

blocks.note: first and last letters only
gripe is an old word for stomach pain, as is colic

explanation.surface: A countryside complaint once the office desk has been emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucolic describes pastoral countryside life, of shepherds and farms, so it means rural.

clue.text: What a big bird has following dinner at the Ritz?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sizeable beak, as on a pelican or toucan
second meaning: the expensive account presented after a meal at a luxury London hotel

explanation.surface: A riddle about what some large creature has after an upmarket meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ritz is a famously expensive London hotel. 'Bill' means both a beak and a restaurant's account.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's beak is its bill, and the account for a lavish restaurant meal is a hefty one.

clue.text: Two embrace five found on a bed  …

definitions.note: a description of where the answer is, not a synonym

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap one's arms round, so one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: a piece for two performers
V is the Roman numeral five

explanation.surface: A pair cuddle up with five others on a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: V goes inside DUET to give DUVET; the ellipsis leads into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A duvet is a quilted bedcover, stuffed with feathers or fibre, lying on top of the mattress.

clue.text: …  therefore organ's flaccid

blocks.note: so means therefore
a newspaper is an organ, here the Financial Times

explanation.surface: Continuing the bedroom scene, a limp body part is the result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests anatomy, but it means a publication; the FT is the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flaccid lacks firmness and hangs limply, which is the opposite of hard.

clue.text: Poet's value of expressions

blocks.note: expressions are terms or phrases
what something is worth

explanation.surface: A judgment on how much a poet's language is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Value of expressions' is read as the expressions' value, so the word for expressions comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet who wrote about daffodils and the Lake District.

clue.text: OTT elite outlandishly attending to appearance

definitions.note: a gerund phrase used as a noun for the process the answer names

indicators.note: doing something outlandishly means in a bizarre, unconventional way, so the letters come out strangely ordered

blocks.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: The over-the-top upper class are fussing absurdly over their looks.
explanation.walkthrough: OTT is short for over the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilette is the process of washing, dressing and grooming oneself, the business of making one's looks presentable.

clue.text: Party animals composed texts about dog

indicators.note: composed means put together or made up, so the letters are assembled in a new order
about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Rover is a stock name for a dog

explanation.surface: Revellers have been writing text messages about a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' looks like calm or written, but it signals that the letters of texts are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Party animals are lively sociable people who love gatherings, the outgoing type psychologists contrast with introverts.

clue.text: Setter clued puzzle for mathematician

indicators.note: puzzle here is a verb, to baffle or muddle, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler writes a puzzle about a famous mathematician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the crossword compiler, so it stands for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Euclid was the ancient Greek geometer whose Elements laid the foundations of geometry.

clue.text: Waits for sexy specs etc (use without frames)

indicators.note: frames surround a picture, so removing them strips each word of its outside letters

blocks.note: inner letters
inner letters
inner letter
inner letter

explanation.surface: Someone waits for stylish glasses but is told to wear them without their frames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frames' suggests spectacle frames, which suits specs, but it means each word loses its first and last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To expect someone is to anticipate their arrival, so waiting for them is the same idea.

clue.text: City's stumble over refined oil

indicators.note: refining a substance processes and alters it, so the letters of the word are reworked

blocks.note: to trip is to stumble
taken as written

explanation.surface: An oil city's stumble over its refined product, a fitting picture for an oil-rich capital.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts TRIP above the rearranged oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is the capital of Libya, a major Mediterranean port and oil-exporting centre.

clue.text: French fry a little bit

blocks.note: first meaning: a stick of fried potato
second meaning: a small fragment broken off

explanation.surface: Just a nibble of a French fry.
explanation.walkthrough: A chip is the British name for a French fry.
explanation.definitionFit: Fried potato sticks are called chips in Britain, and a chip is also a tiny broken piece of something.

clue.text: Bottom of pop singer's hips

definitions.note: plural noun for the singular bone structure

indicators.note: the bottom of a down word is its final letter, so only the last one is kept

blocks.note: its final letter
Elvis Presley, famous for his gyrating hips

explanation.surface: A tribute to the swivelling hips of a pop star, Elvis the Pelvis.
explanation.walkthrough: Elvis Presley was nicknamed Elvis the Pelvis for his hip movements, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelvis is the bony basin that forms the hips, linking the spine to the legs.

clue.text: Squirm from naval war commander (retd)

indicators.note: from means taken out of, so the letters lie inside the run of words that follows
retired means drawn back, so the concealed letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A retired naval commander squirms at memories of war.
explanation.walkthrough: Read naval war commander backwards and the answer appears across the last two words: mmoCRAWLavan.
explanation.definitionFit: To crawl is to wriggle along close to the ground like a worm, a movement close to squirming.

clue.text: Leading law report

indicators.note: a report is something heard, a sound, so we want a word that is pronounced like another

blocks.note: a principle is a fundamental law or rule

explanation.surface: A top story in a legal journal.
explanation.walkthrough: Principle and principal sound the same; only the spelling differs.
explanation.definitionFit: Principal means chief or foremost, the first in importance, which is what leading conveys.

clue.text: Country club hotel is not allowing starters

indicators.note: starters come first in a meal, so the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: C is clubs in card notation
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet
first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A country club hotel refuses to let guests have starters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starters' sounds like the first course of a meal, but it takes the initials of the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: China is the large East Asian nation with the world's second-largest population.

clue.text: Silly nan leaving indication out

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so the letters of one word depart from the other
out here means wrong or disordered, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grandmother wanders off foolishly without giving any sign.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove N, A and N from INDICATION to leave IDICTIO, then rearrange. Nan is a British word for grandmother.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiotic means foolish or stupid, the behaviour of an idiot, so it matches silly.

clue.text: To rig a microphone involves special paperwork

indicators.note: something that involves another thing contains it, so the letters sit inside the words before

blocks.note: spanning the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Wiring someone with a hidden microphone involves special forms to fill in.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run through tO RIG A MIcrophone.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes, playfully described as a particular kind of work with paper.

clue.text: Reckon visitor introduced second couple after one

indicators.note: something introduced is brought inside, so one piece is placed within the other
after places the word for couple behind the word for one

blocks.note: a guest visits
S is the abbreviation for second
I is the Roman numeral one
to couple, as animals do, is to mate

explanation.surface: At a party, a guest is introduced to a second couple after the first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' looks like a noun meaning two people, but it is the verb to mate.
explanation.definitionFit: To guesstimate is to estimate roughly by combining guesswork and calculation, an informal way to reckon.
